sentence: The NHS suggests telling the person you are worried, carrying on as usual, and offering to listen.
Open questions that start with how, what, where or when give the person room to answer in their own words.
The NHS advises against forcing someone to talk or to get help, or going to a GP on their behalf.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.
The NHS suggests telling the person that you are worried about them.
It also suggests carrying on as usual, so the person is not treated differently because of what they are going through.
note: NHS: carry on as usual; second clause paraphrase, flagged for second pass.

sentence: Open questions that start with how, what, where or when are recommended.
The NHS says not to force someone to talk to you.
The NHS gives examples of practical help, such as offering to do the shopping or to go with the person to professional appointments.
It says not to go to a GP on someone's behalf or to force them to get help.
The NHS also says it can be upsetting to hear that someone you care about is in distress, and suggests making time to relax or do something you enjoy.
It adds that looking after your own mental wellbeing helps you support others, and that nobody should feel they must cope alone.

If the difficulties are affecting daily life, the NHS suggests encouraging the person to contact a GP, to get help from NHS 111, or to refer themselves to NHS talking therapies, which is free and does not need an urgent route.
note: NHS: contact a GP, get help from NHS 111, refer themselves for free, non-urgent NHS talking therapy.

sentence: Samaritans and Mind are named as sources of guidance for people who are helping.
The NHS says someone who cannot wait for a doctor, and cannot cope or keep themselves safe, needs urgent support now.
The NHS guidance for people talking about their own mental health suggests choosing someone they trust who can offer the kind of support they need, and planning what to say.
It notes that some people find it easier to talk while walking, travelling in a car or cooking, and that a person does not have to say everything at once.
If the person chosen does not feel able to help, the NHS says not to take it personally.
Looking after someone can be hard, and urgent help is open to carers and friends as well as to the person themselves.
note: Assignment brief: every mental-health page carries the crisis route; trust pages (gmmh urgent-help) list NHS urgent mental health support alongside 999.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E.
note: Trust pages: if life is at risk, someone is in immediate danger or has harmed themselves, call 999 or go to A&E.

sentence: For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf.
note: NHS trust page: call NHS 111 option 2 for urgent mental health support; 24/7; can call for yourself or someone else.

sentence: Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.
note: Samaritans 116 123 free, 24 hours: returned in the urgent-help and NHS grief searches.
